record.file_problem: Full post and comments are present. Some mathematical notation is flattened in the web text, but the prose and reported findings are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests polysemanticity in a trained toy autoencoder using theoretical analysis and experiments, rather than the original neuron-visualization approach.
record.gate_note: The post derives an expected collision rate and reports experiments measuring polysemantic neurons in its toy model. The sparsification simulations that measure l1 norm and estimated nonzero coordinates are not rows because they do not measure polysemanticity. Commenters' proposed experiments are not study results.
record.test_reason: A toy autoencoder with m≥n neurons is trained and polysemantic neurons are counted across widths. It shows polysemanticity arising from random initialization plus l1-driven winner-take-all dynamics without capacity pressure. This bears directly on V4 and argues that V3's superposition story is not the only cause. It is a specific argument that V3 is partial, so T5 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. Random initialization can assign several features to the same neuron, and l1-induced winner-take-all training then locks this in. The result is incidental polysemanticity even when neurons are ample, a second origin alongside superposition. The authors add that it can persist until the neuron count approaches the feature count squared.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a trained, weight-tied toy autoencoder with basis-vector data and l1 activation regularization, plus collision analysis; it does not use the original real-neuron visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported polysemantic-neuron count changes with hidden width m, following a Θ(n²/m) trend. Other architecture and regularization choices are not compared.
record.peer_reviewed: Alignment Forum post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The evidence is limited to a simplified toy model with basis-vector data and l1 activation regularization, which the authors note is uncommon. The authors say the theory for interactions among all three training forces is incomplete. No uncertainty estimates or explicit control comparisons are reported, and the empirical result is stated as an aggregate trend rather than per-width values.
record.rows_left_out: The sparsification simulations and their predicted l1-norm/nonzero-coordinate trajectories are omitted because they do not measure polysemanticity. See “Numerical simulations.”

untested.parts: No condition with more features than neurons (m<n) is run, so superposition-driven polysemanticity is not itself measured. The share of polysemanticity due to each mechanism in real networks is not measured.

Only l1 activation regularization with basis-vector data in one toy autoencoder is tested. Not tested: other winner-take-all sources (activation nonlinearities, layer norm), co-occurring features, and real networks.

missing.what: Per-width counts of polysemantic neurons versus hidden width, shown in the 'Polysemantic neurons vs hidden neurons' graph and the notebook. Only the qualitative fit is stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The post is preliminary, with no uncertainty reported. The l1 regularization is needed to create a privileged basis, and the authors admit it is uncommon. A commenter (Rohin Shah) argues the result may depend on features never co-occurring; this is untested. The verdicts treat 'challenges' for V3 as too strong, because the study shows an additional cause rather than an absence of superposition-driven polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or vision-model neurons are studied.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, tokens, or contexts are studied.
The post gives a toy-model counterexample to superposition as a necessary cause; it does not establish how often either mechanism occurs in real networks.
Tests random initialization and training in the specified toy setup, not other sources such as regularization or training noise across other models.
Uses l1 regularization in one setup; does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization choices, or measure a performance cost of reducing polysemanticity.
Does not re-examine canonical real-network neurons or test whether their apparently unrelated inputs share a feature.
Does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

tranche.reason: The post presents a second, non-exclusive origin of polysemanticity (not superposition), so V3 needs restating. It uses a different method (toy model plus theory). T2 is also defensible for V4.

source_check.notes: Victor Lecomte post; the contributions section names Kushal, Trevor and Rylan, so it is likely the same work as arXiv:2312.03096 and not independent of it. Basis-vector data means features never co-occur. There is no run without l1 or with varied lambda. In a comment reply the author says that without l1 every neuron would carry weight for every feature (no privileged basis), so the post does not isolate l1 as a producer of polysemanticity. The text gives only the trend and the 1/4 constant, not per-width counts.

statements.problem: Post poses the necessary vs incidental question in real networks as open, which matches.
Independence of the two records is not established by the text here.
